content: Eduardo Franco has been involved in advisory board meetings and forums organized by Merck, Roche, and Gen-Probe, focusing on strategies for cervical cancer prevention, including HPV vaccines and HPV tests. Over the past four years, he has received an average honorarium of $4,000 per company for these activities. However, none of the funders had any role in the collection, analysis, or interpretation of the data. Julia Gage, as part of her work with the United States National Cancer Institute (NCI) under the National Institutes of Health (NIH), conducted an operations research project in Nigeria to evaluate the effectiveness of the careHPV screening test manufactured by Qiagen. Qiagen provided the reagents, equipment, and supplies for the study, while the NCI funded all other aspects of the research. Francisco Garcia served as the principal investigator for drug trials involving novel agents for cervical cancer treatment during his tenure at the University of Arizona. These trials were conducted under research contracts with Roche ($150,000), Inovio ($70,000), Photocure ($120,000), and Roche/Ventana ($100,000). Garcia did not receive any personal income from these trials. José Jeronimo is an employee of PATH, an international non-profit organization dedicated to developing and delivering high-impact, low-cost tools for global health. PATH has collaborated with Qiagen to develop a rapid HPV test (careHPV) and with Arbor Vita to create a rapid test for cervical cancer screening (targeting E6 and E7 oncoproteins). PATH received samples and equipment from both companies to validate these tests in various countries. The PATH-Qiagen agreement prioritizes the commercialization of the test in China and India, with other countries included based on regional conditions. These tests will be made available at low cost to the public sector in low-resource countries. Enriquito Lu was the principal investigator for an HPV vaccination study conducted by Jhpiego, an international non-profit organization, under an agreement with Merck. The study aimed to assess the feasibility and acceptability of integrating HPV vaccination for girls aged 9–13 into cervical cancer prevention programs for mothers in Thailand and the Philippines. Merck provided $850,000 and HPV vaccines for up to 4,000 girls at each project site. Lu did not receive any personal income for his work on this study. Raul Murillo worked as a consultant for GSK to analyze the cost-effectiveness of the HPV vaccine. Swee Chong Quek has participated in advisory board meetings and speaker forums organized by GSK and Qiagen over the past four years. These events focused on cervical cancer prevention strategies, HPV vaccine efficacy studies, and the clinical relevance of HPV vaccination for preventing cervical cancer and other HPV-related diseases. Quek received a total combined income of S$9,000 (Singapore dollars) for these activities. Achim Schneider serves as an advisor to Karl Storz, contributing to the development of laparoscopic techniques and instruments for treating cervical cancer and other diseases. He receives an annual honorarium of €40,000 for this role. Schneider has also participated in advisory board meetings and lectures on HPV vaccination organized by GSK and Sanofi, for which he received a total combined income of $20,000 over the past four years. Vivien Tsu, an employee of PATH, has been involved in large-scale demonstration projects for cervical cancer prevention, screening, and treatment in developing countries. PATH received donated vaccines from GSK and Merck and careHPV tests from Qiagen for these projects. Tsu also participated in an alternative-dose-schedule study in Vietnam, for which PATH received donated vaccines from Merck.
